studies.title: Out Of The Darknesses
studies.meaning: The surah opens by saying what a book is for: to bring people out. Darkness is plural in the Arabic and light is singular. Early scholars note this without making too much of it, since the same pairing runs through the Quran. Two qualifications follow at once. It happens by the permission of their Lord, so the messenger is the instrument and not the cause. The destination is named twice, first as a path and then as the one whose path it is.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a time when most of the city refused the message and its listeners were a minority under pressure. No occasion is reported for these ayat. Early scholars note that the surah takes its name from Abraham, although he is named only once in it. They also note that its opening addresses the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) directly. The statement of purpose comes before any argument begins.

keyTerms.note: A plural, from the root that also gives the word for wrongdoing. Arabic can make darkness plural because there are many kinds of it. The Quran never makes plural the light that answers them.
A qualification set into the middle of the messenger's task. It keeps the bringing out from being something a human being achieves, while leaving his instruction fully in place.
A pair occurring three times in the Quran. The first name is about power nobody can touch. The second is about being worthy of praise, so might is joined to goodness rather than standing alone.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Night in the desert was genuinely dark and genuinely dangerous. Travellers waited for the moon and camps kept fires going. Being caught out between settlements after sunset could cost a man his life or his direction. Light was not a comfortable image in that world. It was the difference between arriving and not arriving. Everyone hearing this knew the relief of a fire seen from a distance.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about bringing people out of the darknesses into the light occurs seven times in the Quran. Two of them are in this surah, within five ayat of each other. The first describes the Book given to the Prophet. The second describes the signs given to Moses, in identical wording.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is defined here by its effect rather than by its content. It is a thing that moves people from one condition to another. That makes reading it an event rather than a gathering of information. The permission clause matters just as much. Human effort is real, and it is an instrument. The outcome is not in the hands of the one making the effort, which steadies anyone who tries to help another person change.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the identical phrase about darkness and light, applied to Moses and his people.
Describes God as the ally of believers, bringing them out of darkness into light.
Uses the same formula of a messenger sent with clear signs to bring people out.

studies.applyIt: Notice one small thing you already know is a step out of something. It might be a message you have been avoiding, or a habit you know well. Do it today rather than resolving to do it. The ayah describes bringing out as a movement. A movement starts at a set hour, not in general.
studies.explainEasier: God gave this book to his messenger for one job. The job is to lead people out of the dark and into the light. That only happens when God allows it. The road leads to God himself.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Preferring The Nearer Life
studies.meaning: The verb is the interesting part. They do not reject the hereafter; they hold this life dearer. That is a matter of preference rather than of doctrine. Two more activities follow: turning others away from the path, and wanting that path crooked. Early scholars note the progression. A private preference becomes interference with other people. Then it becomes an active wish that the road itself were less straight. What began as an appetite ends as a project.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The leading families of the city had built their standing on trade, on the pilgrimage and on inherited position. The new message unsettled all three, so their objection was practical before it was theological. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars describe the setting in general terms. They note that the ayah does not accuse anyone of denying the hereafter outright, only of preferring what is nearer.

keyTerms.note: A form meaning to seek out and prefer what one loves. The root is love itself. So the description is about affection rather than belief, which makes it uncomfortably easy to recognise.
The adjective means lower or closer rather than worldly. The contrast built into the phrase is one of distance. This life is the near one and the other is further off, not false against true.
A turn away from straightness, used of a road, a stick or a character. Wanting the path crooked means wanting the standard adjusted. That is a different complaint from saying the standard is false.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan wealth was built on things you could see: caravans arriving, a season's profit, standing at the shrine, a name people knew. The hereafter offered nothing to weigh against those in the present tense. The ayah speaks of preferring the nearer life. It is describing men who could point at what they would lose and could not point at what they were being offered.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for the present life means the nearer or lower one. Its root is about closeness rather than about the material world. Its opposite, used throughout the Quran, simply means the later one. So the whole contrast in Arabic is between near and far in time. Neither term implies that the near one is unreal.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts the problem in what a person loves rather than in what they assert. That is a harder diagnosis to escape. Someone can hold every correct belief and still be described by this ayah. It also traces how preference becomes obstruction. A man who prefers the near life has an interest in nobody else choosing differently, since a visible alternative is itself a kind of pressure.

crossReferences.why: The other side of the same contrast: God makes the believers firm in this life and the next.
States the preference plainly as a human habit, and says the later life is better and lasting.
Uses the same word for wanting the path crooked, in a description of those turned away.

studies.applyIt: Look at your calendar for last week rather than at your beliefs. Add up roughly where the hours went. Do not judge the total, since most of it had to happen. Just find one hour that did not. Give that hour to something that only makes sense if the further life is real. One hour, once, this week.
studies.explainEasier: These people love this life more than the next one. They also try to stop other people from following God's road. They want that road to be bent, so it is not straight any more.

studies.title: In The Tongue Of His People
studies.meaning: A rule with no exceptions is stated in half a sentence. No messenger was ever sent except in the language of his own people. The reason given is equally plain: so that he could make things clear to them. Early scholars note that the word for language is literally tongue. They note that the principle covers more than vocabulary, since a messenger shared his hearers' idiom, their references and their way of arguing. The second half of the ayah then places guidance and misguidance beyond the messenger's reach entirely.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran's Arabic was itself an argument in that setting. Scripture was associated with other languages and other communities, and its opponents could not claim they had failed to understand it. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars connect it to the wider Meccan objection that a true revelation should have arrived in some grander form.

keyTerms.gloss: in the tongue of his people
keyTerms.note: The word is the physical tongue, used for language as English uses it in mother tongue. The phrase occurs only here in the Quran, in the ayah that makes it a rule for every messenger.

keyTerms.gloss: so that he may make clear
keyTerms.note: From the root behind the word for clarity in the surrounding surahs. Making clear is named as the purpose of the sending. That makes obscurity a failure of the mission rather than a mark of depth.
Placed immediately after the clarity clause. Early scholars read the order as deliberate: everything a messenger can control is done first, and only then is the outcome handed back to God.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia was full of languages that people did not share. Traders dealt with Persian, Aramaic and Greek speakers on the roads north. Scripture existed in tongues most Meccans could not read. A man's own dialect marked which tribe he came from within a few words. Being addressed in your own speech, with no interpreter and no learned go-between, was a specific and unusual kind of respect.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah's phrase about a messenger sent in the tongue of his own people occurs only once in the Quran. It is stated as a rule without exceptions, covering every messenger ever sent. The verse two surahs earlier makes the matching claim about this Book in particular. It says the Book was sent as an Arabic recitation so that its hearers might reason.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is committed to being understood, and the commitment is universal rather than a concession to one audience. That has consequences for how scripture is handled. A reading that needs the text to be obscure runs against the reason given here for how it was sent. The ayah also divides the labour cleanly. Clarity is the messenger's task. What happens inside a listener is not, and the second half says so before anyone can take credit or blame.

crossReferences.why: Makes the matching claim about this Book: sent as an Arabic recitation so that you may reason.
Answers the objection directly by imagining a non-Arabic Quran sent to Arabic speakers.
Names the messenger's task as making clear to people what has been sent down to them.

studies.applyIt: Take something you know well and explain it once this week to someone outside your field. Use their words rather than yours, with no shortcuts through jargon. If you cannot, that is information about your own understanding rather than about them. That is the uncomfortable and useful half of this exercise.
studies.explainEasier: God always sent a messenger who spoke the same language as his own people. That way he could explain things to them clearly. After that, it is God who decides who finds the right way.

studies.title: Remind Them Of God's Days
studies.meaning: Moses is sent with the same task the surah opened with, word for word. Bring your people out of the darknesses into the light. A second instruction is added, and it is unusual. Remind them of the Days of God. Early scholars explain the phrase as the occasions when God acted decisively in a people's history. That covers rescue and reckoning alike. They note that remembering is treated as work, not as a mood. The ayah closes by naming who takes the signs: everyone patient and thankful.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The account of Moses was the Quran's most often told history. Its Meccan audience recognised in it a small community under a powerful state. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars observe that this surah gives Moses only a few ayat. It uses his commission mainly to show that the task named at the surah's opening is not new, and that the same words were given before.

keyTerms.note: A phrase occurring twice in the Quran. Early scholars read the days as the great turning points where God's dealing with a people became visible. That covers deliverance and judgement alike.
An intensified form of the verb to remember, meaning to make someone else remember. The Quran treats reminding as a separate office. People do not lose what they know so much as stop attending to it.
Two intensive forms paired, one for enduring and one for giving thanks. The combination occurs four times in the Quran. It always names those who can actually read what has been shown them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A people without writing kept its past in named days. Battles, droughts and deliverances each had a name. Reciting them was how a tribe knew who it was. The Arabs called these the days of the Arabs and could list them for generations. Telling Moses to remind his people of the Days of God uses exactly that habit. It changes whose acts are being recited.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction given to Moses here repeats the purpose stated for the Book in this surah's first ayah, word for word. The same phrase about darkness and light is applied twice within five ayat. Once to a scripture given in Arabia, and once to signs given in Egypt. That is how the surah says the mission is one thing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Memory is presented as a religious faculty rather than a private one. Forgetting is the ordinary danger. The pairing at the end explains why. Signs are legible to people who can both endure and give thanks. Those are the two responses that keep attention open in bad times and good. Someone with neither will pass the same events and read nothing in them.

crossReferences.why: The identical phrase about darkness and light, applied to the Book rather than to Moses.
Moses carries out the instruction, reminding his people of a specific deliverance.
Uses the same pair, steadfast and thankful, of those who read the signs at sea.

studies.applyIt: Write down three dates that were turning points in your own life. Give one line each about what happened and who you think arranged it. Keep the list. Most people can name their difficulties instantly and have to work to recall their rescues. That imbalance is what this instruction is aimed at.
studies.explainEasier: God sent Moses to lead his people out of the dark and into the light. He also told Moses to remind them of the days when God acted. People who wait patiently and say thank you see these signs.

studies.title: Remember When He Delivered You
studies.meaning: Moses does what he was told to do in the ayah before, and the reminder is specific. Not that God is good to you, but that He took you out of the hands of one household doing particular things. The details are named without softening: sons killed, daughters spared. Then comes a phrase the early scholars pause on. The whole situation is called a great trial from your Lord. Scholars differ over whether the trial is the oppression or the rescue, and the Arabic allows both.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The community around the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) included people being physically abused by their own clans for accepting the message. The account of an oppressed group that was finally delivered spoke directly into that. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars treat the events named as the well-known history of the Israelites in Egypt.

keyTerms.note: A command in the plural, addressed to a whole people. Remembrance in the Quran is usually done on purpose and out loud. It is closer to reciting a history than to a private act of recall.
The verb first describes putting animals out to pasture and driving them. So the image is of a people herded into suffering as a matter of routine, rather than in a single episode.

The word covers both hardship and blessing, since both test a person. That double sense is why the early scholars differ over whether this ayah calls the oppression or the deliverance the great trial.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian society knew servitude at close range. It knew what a strong tribe could do to a weak one with no protector. Killing the sons of a subject group and keeping the daughters was a known way of ending a people without ending its usefulness. Nobody hearing this needed the mechanics explained. What they may have needed was the reminder that such a situation had once been reversed.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for a trial is used elsewhere in the Quran for good fortune as readily as for hardship. That is why the classical commentaries divide over what is being called a great trial here. Arabic keeps ease and hardship inside one term, because both put a person to the test. English needs two different words to carry what this one holds.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Gratitude is grounded in history rather than in feeling. What is asked for is the calling to mind of specific events. That can be done whether or not a person feels grateful, and the feeling is expected to follow the act rather than come first. The ayah also refuses to tidy away the suffering. The deliverance is remembered together with what was delivered from, in the same breath.

crossReferences.why: The instruction Moses is carrying out here, to remind his people of the Days of God.
The declaration that follows immediately, attaching increase to thanks.
Recounts the same deliverance in nearly identical wording, addressed to a later generation.

studies.applyIt: Tell one story of rescue at your next family meal: something that went badly and then did not. It can be from your own life or from a generation above you. Say who you think arranged it. Households repeat their grievances without prompting, and have to be deliberate about the other kind of story.
studies.explainEasier: Moses tells his people to remember what God did for them. A cruel ruler was killing their baby boys and letting the girls live. God saved them from him. That was a huge test.

studies.title: If You Give Thanks
studies.meaning: The promise is put with unusual force. The verb behind proclaimed carries a formal announcement. Both halves are strengthened by oath words that English cannot show. Early scholars point out the lopsided shape. The increase is stated plainly, and its size is left open. The cost of ingratitude is not spelled out as a taking away. It is named as severity. Thanks are placed as the cause, not as the reward.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The words sit inside a speech of Moses to the Israelites, recalling their rescue from Pharaoh. The framing matters. They are quoted as something their Lord announced to them. So a reader in Mecca hears a promise already made to an earlier people, and finds it addressed to him. The surah belongs to the years of pressure before the migration, when the community had little visible increase to count.

keyTerms.note: Built from the root for hearing and permission. The form suggests a public announcement made binding by being declared, closer to a herald's proclamation than to a private promise.
The root also describes an animal that grows visibly well on little fodder, and an udder that fills. Thankfulness in Arabic is something that shows in the body, not only a feeling held privately.
The root means to cover over. It is the same word used for rejecting faith, and the overlap is deliberate: hiding a benefit you received and denying the one who gave it are treated as one movement.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Increase was the main worry of a herding economy. A flock either grew through a season or it did not. The gap between a family that ate and one that borrowed came down to lambs living and rain arriving. Debt in Mecca ran through the same channels as family ties. So a bad year cost standing as well as animals. A promise worded as increase landed on people who counted everything.
studies.didYouKnow: The second half of the sentence does not complete the parallel. Where the first says if you thank, I will increase you, the second does not say and if you are ungrateful I will decrease you. It shifts speaker and subject, moving from I to My punishment. Early scholars have long noticed the break and read it as mercy holding the sentence open.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Gratitude is put forward as a working cause, not as good manners. The link between what a person owns up to and what they are given is stated as a rule. God binds Himself to it by announcing it, which is stronger than a general assurance. At the same time, no amount is given. The reader learns that thanks make a difference, without being told what the increase will be or when. That keeps the practice from turning into a trade.

crossReferences.why: Names the limit the thanking runs into: the blessings cannot be counted at all.
Says gratitude returns to the grateful, since God has no need of it.
Solomon draws the same conclusion from a gift, testing whether he will thank or be ungrateful.

studies.applyIt: Tonight, before you sleep, name three things from today out loud, and make them small: the water was hot, someone let you merge, your knee did not hurt. Out loud matters, because the word for thanks in this passage is about something that shows. Do it for a week and see whether the list gets easier to fill.
studies.explainEasier: God makes a promise here. If you thank him for what you have, he will give you more. If you refuse to thank him and act as if it never came from him, his punishment is hard.

studies.title: Even If Everyone Refused
studies.meaning: Moses removes an assumption buried inside the declaration before it. If thanks brings increase, a listener may conclude that God needs the thanks. So the case is put at its largest. Even if you and everyone on earth together were ungrateful, God is free of need and worthy of praise. Early scholars note the pairing of the two names. Being independent of creation could sound like indifference. The second name blocks that reading by keeping praiseworthiness in the sentence.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The gods of the shrine were understood as needing attention: offerings, upkeep, visits, a share of the trade. A god who required nothing at all was a genuinely unfamiliar idea, and this ayah states it in the strongest terms available. No occasion is reported for it. Early scholars read it as the necessary corrective to the promise of increase in the ayah before.

keyTerms.note: The word for a rich man, one who has no want of anyone. Applied to God it removes any transaction from worship. Nothing offered can add to Him, and nothing withheld can take anything away.
A form meaning both praised and praiseworthy. It closes the door on the coldness the first name might imply. Independence here is not detachment but a goodness that does not depend on being noticed.

The root means to cover something over, and it carries both ingratitude and denial. Burying a benefit and denying a truth are one act in this vocabulary. That is why the two senses are hard to separate.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every relationship in that society ran on obligation. A patron protected a client, and the client owed him support. A shrine received gifts and returned standing. A guest was fed and was bound by it afterwards. Nobody gave without a return being understood. The claim that God gains nothing at all from human thanks removed worship from the only economy the audience had.
studies.didYouKnow: The pair of names closing this ayah, free of need and worthy of praise, occurs four times in the Quran. Most of those passages are about giving: charity offered, or thanks rendered. The formula tends to appear where the Book is guarding against one idea. That idea is that God profits from what people hand over.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Worship is relocated entirely to the worshipper's side. If nothing reaches God, then gratitude is done for the sake of what it makes of a person. That is also how the promise of increase in the ayah before should be read. The passage makes divine independence a comfort rather than a distance. A God who needs nothing has no interest to serve in what He commands.

crossReferences.why: The declaration this ayah qualifies, promising increase to those who give thanks.
States the relation directly: you are the ones in need, and God is the Free of need.
Uses the same pair of names to close an instruction about giving from what is good.

studies.applyIt: Do one act of worship this week without asking it to do anything for you. No calm expected, no problem being solved, no streak being kept. Just the act, offered, with nothing attached. Notice how much of your usual practice turns out to have had an errand in it.
studies.explainEasier: Moses says that God does not need our thanks. If everyone on earth stopped saying thank you, God would lose nothing at all. He is rich in himself, and he is still worth praising.

studies.title: None Knows Them But God
studies.meaning: Three peoples are named, and then the list is cut off with a clause that changes its character. And those after them, whom none knows but God. History is admitted to be larger than what has been kept. What survives is the pattern, and the ayah states it in one sentence. Messengers came with clear proofs, and the response was a gesture and a refusal. The gesture is described in words the early scholars read several ways, and none of the readings is a welcome.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Noah, Aad and Thamud were the standard examples in Meccan preaching. Traders passed the ruins linked with the last two on the roads north. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars note that naming three and then declining to name the rest puts the Meccan audience inside a sequence rather than opposite it. They too would one day be among those after them.

keyTerms.note: A clause admitting that most of human history is unrecorded. It does not say the record was lost. It says the knowledge is with God, which is a claim about where such things are kept.

keyTerms.gloss: they put their hands to mouths
keyTerms.note: The early scholars explain the gesture in several ways: biting the hand in rage, gesturing for silence, or covering the mouth in scorn. All the readings agree it is a refusal to hear rather than an argument.
A participle from a root beside doubt itself. It is held to the very end of the ayah, far from the noun it describes. The doubt it names is not calm uncertainty. It unsettles the doubter.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Arabs kept genealogy and famous days by memory, and could recite generations without error. They also knew the limits of that record. Beyond a certain distance the names stopped. Ruins in the north and south belonged to peoples nobody could account for. The ayah admits that most of the past is unknown, which would have matched what a well-informed listener already suspected.
studies.didYouKnow: The gesture described in this ayah, hands returned to mouths, has no agreed meaning in the classical commentaries. They record several possibilities without choosing between them. It is one of a small number of places where the tradition keeps an image. The exact sense of that image was already uncertain to the earliest interpreters.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Refusal is shown as a physical act before it is an argument. The people in this ayah do not answer the proofs. They make a gesture, state a rejection and describe their own condition as doubt. The passage also sets a limit on human knowledge of history, while insisting the pattern inside it can be read. That is how the Quran generally uses the past: not as a chronicle but as a demonstration.

crossReferences.why: The messengers' reply to this refusal, which begins by questioning whether the doubt is real.
Sends the listener to look at the ruins of earlier peoples rather than argue about them.
Says plainly that messengers were sent whose stories were not related to the Prophet at all.

studies.applyIt: Notice a gesture you make when you do not want to hear something: the phone picked up, the half-turn away, the laugh. Catch it once this week and stay still instead. You do not have to agree with whatever is being said. The exercise is only to let the sentence finish.
studies.explainEasier: The Quran names three old peoples and says there were many more that only God knows about. Messengers came to them with clear proof. The people put their hands to their mouths and said no.

studies.title: Is There Doubt About God
studies.meaning: The messengers answer a refusal with a question and a name. Is there doubt about God, the Originator of the heavens and the earth. The argument is not developed. The name is the argument. Then the invitation is described in two clauses. He calls you so that He may forgive you, and so that He may put you off to a stated term. The reply is an objection to the messengers rather than to the claim: you are only human beings like us.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Meccans accepted a creator and disputed the messenger, which is exactly the shape of the exchange reported here. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars note that the demand for a clear authority at the end was the standing Meccan request for a miracle on demand. The surah answers it in the next ayah rather than by producing one.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to split open, as a seed splits or a shoot breaks the soil. Creation in this word is a bringing forth from nothing, not a shaping of what was there.

keyTerms.gloss: so that He may forgive you
keyTerms.note: Named as the purpose of the calling, before anything is asked. The root means to cover over. So what the invitation offers first is the covering of what is there, rather than a set of demands.
A deadline already named. The promise is not endless life but the full allotted span. That is a modest offer, and the Quran repeats it wherever it is careful about what is being promised.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everyone in Arabia farmed, herded or traded in things that grew. The splitting of a seed was the most ordinary miracle available. Date palms came from stones, barley from grain, a whole season's food from something small enough to lose. The name used here for God comes from exactly that image. So the argument the messengers make is drawn from what their hearers handled every day.
studies.didYouKnow: The divine name used here, the Originator of the heavens and the earth, occurs six times in the Quran. It gives one surah its title. One of the six is the closing prayer of the previous surah, where Joseph uses it in thanks. So the same name appears in neighbouring surahs. It stands once in a prayer of gratitude and once in an argument against doubt.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The messengers begin from what their audience already accepts, rather than from what is disputed. The passage also describes the shape of a call from God. Forgiveness is offered first, then time is granted, and no demand is stated in this ayah at all. The objection that comes back is instructive too. It concerns the messenger's ordinariness rather than anything he has actually said.

crossReferences.why: Joseph uses the same divine name of origination in the prayer that closes his story.
The messengers' reply, which concedes the objection entirely and then answers it.
Opens a surah with the same name, joined to the angels and their wings.

studies.applyIt: Pick up something that grew: a seed, a date stone, an onion starting to sprout in a drawer. Hold it for a minute and follow the actual sequence backwards. The name in this ayah comes from that image. The argument the messengers make is one you can perform with your hands rather than only read.
studies.explainEasier: The messengers ask how anyone can doubt God, who made the sky and the earth from nothing. God is calling people so he can forgive them and give them more time. The people answer that the messengers are only men.

studies.title: We Are Only Human Like You
studies.meaning: The objection is granted in full before it is answered. We are only human beings like you, the messengers say. That concedes everything the complaint contained. What they add is not a claim about themselves. It is a claim about God's freedom to favour whom He wills among His servants. The demand for a proof on request is then declined in the same spirit. Producing one is not in our power without God's leave. The ayah then turns from argument to posture, and the posture is reliance.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The demand that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) produce a sign to order is recorded again and again in the Quran. This ayah gives an earlier generation's answer to the same demand. No occasion is reported for it. Early scholars note that the messengers make no counter-claim to being better, which fits how the Quran presents prophethood throughout.

keyTerms.note: The word for a human being as a physical creature, with skin and hunger. Messengers in the Quran accept this description rather than resisting it. Their whole usefulness depends on it.

The verb for giving a favour freely. Placing the choice with God removes any suggestion that the messengers were picked for merit. That would have made the objection about their ordinariness stronger, not weaker.

keyTerms.gloss: let them rely, let them entrust
keyTerms.note: An imperative in the third person, closing the sentence with an instruction rather than a claim. The same formula ends the following ayah too, so the exchange resolves twice into the same word.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Authority in that world came with visible marks: a lineage, wealth, armed followers, a place at the assembly. A man asking to be believed without any of them was making an unusual request. The natural response was to ask what made him different. The messengers answer that nothing does. That leaves the whole weight of the case on what they are saying rather than on who is saying it.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction to rely on God closes this ayah and the next one in almost identical words, twice in a row. The same formula appears again in the previous surah, where a father sends his sons to Egypt. Three uses within a few pages attach the phrase to two situations. One is messengers under threat, the other a parent letting go of a child.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates the messenger from the message with unusual clarity. Ordinariness is admitted. Selection is placed entirely with God. The power to produce proofs is denied to the human being altogether. What is left is reliance. It is offered not as consolation but as the practical position of people who have just conceded that the outcome is not theirs to arrange.

crossReferences.why: Continues the same speech, ending on the identical instruction to rely on God.
The same closing formula, spoken by a father sending his sons on a dangerous journey.
The demand for a marvel answered by the same admission: I am only a human messenger.

studies.applyIt: Think of a case you are making that you have been propping up with your own credentials. Try it once this week on the strength of the reasons alone, without mentioning your experience or position. If it holds, you have learned something. If it does not, that is worth knowing before you lean on it further.
studies.explainEasier: The messengers agree that they are just people, the same as everyone else. God chooses whoever he wants. They cannot make a miracle happen on their own. So they put their trust in God.

studies.title: We Will Bear Your Harm
studies.meaning: The reason given for reliance is a debt already owed. Why would we not rely on Him, when He has guided us in our ways. Then comes the commitment, stated with the strongest emphasis Arabic has. We will certainly endure the harm you do us. Early scholars note that endurance is promised in advance, not reported afterwards. They note the harm is named as continuing rather than past. The ayah ends where the one before ended, on the same word for entrusting an outcome to God.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from years when members of the community were beaten, boycotted and cut off by their own families. The question of how long to keep enduring was live rather than theoretical. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars read the messengers' answer as the pattern for anyone in that position: state the reason, name the endurance, and hand over the result.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for paths, so guidance covers the various roads a person actually walks rather than one road. The verb takes two objects, which is how Arabic marks being shown the way.

Two emphatic markers, one before the verb and one after. That is the strongest oath-like construction available. Endurance is being undertaken rather than described, in the manner of a formal commitment.

keyTerms.gloss: the harm you have done us
keyTerms.note: The root covers injury that wounds without destroying: insult, obstruction, mistreatment. It is the Quran's usual word for what a community suffers from its neighbours, rather than for open warfare.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Harm in that setting had a particular texture. A man's goods were left unbought in the market. His greeting went unreturned, his daughter's marriage was refused, rubbish was left at his door, his own clan withdrew its protection. It was not usually a single blow but a hundred small exclusions, sustained for years. It was designed to make ordinary life impossible rather than to end it.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the one before it both close on the same instruction to rely on God. The words are nearly the same twice in a row. The Quran rarely repeats a formula in neighbouring ayat like this. Here it does so at the end of a speech about being threatened with expulsion. The doubling falls exactly where the pressure is greatest.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Endurance is presented as a reasoned position rather than a temperament. The messengers give their ground first, which is guidance already received. Only then do they commit to bearing what follows. That order matters. Patience without a reason is only stamina, and it runs out. The ayah also treats reliance and endurance as belonging together, since a person who has handed over the outcome has less to defend.

crossReferences.why: The threat this endurance is answering, delivered immediately afterwards as expulsion or return.
The first half of the same speech, ending on the identical instruction about reliance.
Tells a later community it will hear much that hurts, and names endurance as the resolve required.

studies.applyIt: If you are enduring something, write down the reason in one sentence. Keep it somewhere you will see it. Not an encouragement, a reason. People rarely run out of strength before they run out of the thread joining what they bear to why. This ayah puts its reason first for that purpose.
studies.explainEasier: The messengers say they trust God because he has already shown them the way. They promise to put up with the harm people do to them. Then they say again that they rely on God.

studies.title: Leave Our Land Or Return
studies.meaning: The argument ends and the ultimatum begins. Two options are offered, expulsion or a return to the ancestral way. Both treat belief as a matter of belonging rather than of truth. The reply does not come from the messengers. It arrives as revelation over their heads: We will destroy the wrongdoers. Early scholars note the shift in who is speaking. They note that the answer to a threat about land is itself about land. The next ayah promises the same ground to the people being driven off it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Expulsion was the sharpest instrument that society had. The community around the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) had already sent members abroad, and would soon face a boycott and then departure from the city. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars note that the threat is put by the disbelievers to their own messengers, which places the conflict inside communities rather than between them.

keyTerms.gloss: we will surely drive you out
keyTerms.note: An emphatic construction. The verb comes from the same root as the bringing out in this surah's first ayah. One root covers being drawn from darkness to light and being expelled from your country.
The word for going back to something earlier. It assumes the messengers had once belonged to the ancestral way. So the demand is framed as a return home rather than as a conversion.

keyTerms.gloss: so their Lord revealed to them
keyTerms.note: The answer bypasses the argument entirely, and is addressed to the messengers rather than to the people threatening them. What follows is not an instruction but an announcement about what will happen.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man expelled from his territory lost everything at once. He lost the wells his people used, the market where he was known, the protection that made travel possible, and the graves of his family. There was no neutral ground to move to. Arabian listeners would have understood expulsion as a sentence of destitution or death. It was delivered without anyone having to raise a hand.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb the threat uses for driving people out comes from the same root as this surah's opening ayah. That ayah speaks of bringing humanity out of darkness into light. Within thirteen ayat the Book uses one root twice. It covers the purpose of revelation and the punishment threatened against those who carry it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two visions of belonging are set against each other in one sentence. For the threat-makers, a person's place in the land depends on holding the community's creed. The answer transfers the tenure entirely, making it depend on how a person stands before God. The passage also shows a threat answered without a counter-threat from the messengers. What they receive is information, not a weapon.

crossReferences.why: The rest of the answer, promising the land to those who fear God's presence and warning.
The bringing out this surah opened with, using the same root as the expulsion threatened here.
The identical ultimatum put to an earlier prophet: leave our town or come back to our way.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you have been offered a version of this choice: fit in with us, or be outside. It is rarely stated as plainly as it is here. When you find one, name it accurately to yourself, including what you would actually lose. Clarity about the price is what makes a decision yours rather than a drift.
studies.explainEasier: The people threaten the messengers. They say: leave our land, or come back to the way our fathers followed. God answers the messengers himself. He says he will destroy the people who do wrong.

studies.title: Whoever Fears My Standing
studies.meaning: The promise of the land is made and then narrowed by a condition stated twice: for whoever fears My standing, and fears My warning. Early scholars read the first phrase as awe at being placed before God. They note that fear here qualifies a person for a gift rather than threatening them with loss. Then comes the outcome of the other side, told in two short ayat. They prayed for victory, every stubborn tyrant was disappointed, and what waits beyond him is described by his drink.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The community hearing this had been threatened with expulsion. They had no land, no numbers and no protector strong enough to promise them anything. No occasion is reported for these ayat. Early scholars note that the request for victory in the second of these ayat is read in two ways, as made by the messengers or by their opponents. The outcome named settles who was answered.

keyTerms.note: The noun means a place of standing. Early scholars read it as the position a person occupies before God. So what is feared is not harm but an account given face to face.

The first word describes someone who forces others to his will, the second one who refuses to yield to evidence. The pair occurs twice in the Quran, and both times names a human posture rather than an office.
The second word names the matter that seeps from a wound. Putting it beside the word for water makes the phrase a contradiction in terms. That is the effect intended, and it occurs only here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water decided everything. A tribe's standing was measured by the wells it controlled. Hospitality began with a drink. The worst thing that could happen on a journey was reaching water that had gone bad. Every listener had tasted a bad well and knew the particular despair of arriving at one. The image in these ayat uses that experience rather than describing anything unfamiliar.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing what the tyrant is given to drink occurs only once in the Quran. It joins the ordinary word for water to a word for the discharge from a wound. Arabic can build such a phrase without softening either term. So the expression stays deliberately unresolved rather than becoming a simple name for a bad drink.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Fear is presented here as a qualification rather than a burden. The people promised the land are named by what they hold in awe. That makes the inheritance a matter of orientation rather than of strength or numbers. The passage also declines to make tyranny impressive. The overbearing man is answered not by a greater force in this world but by disappointment. That is a smaller and more exact word.

crossReferences.why: The threat of expulsion that these ayat answer by promising the same land to the threatened.
Promises gardens to whoever fears standing before their Lord, using the same phrase.
The only other use of the pair naming a stubborn tyrant, applied to a people who refused a prophet.

studies.applyIt: Try naming, once this week, what you are actually afraid of when you avoid doing something you know is right. Usually it is a person's reaction rather than any consequence. This passage puts a different figure in that position. Say the sentence about standing before God once, and see whether the other fear shrinks slightly.
studies.explainEasier: God promises the land to people who stand in awe of him. They asked for victory. Every proud, stubborn ruler was let down. What is waiting for a cruel ruler is a drink no one could want.

studies.title: Death From Every Direction
studies.meaning: The ayah describes an act that will not complete. He gulps it and can barely get it down. Death comes at him from everywhere and he does not die. Early scholars note the grammar of the first verb. It describes swallowing in repeated small efforts rather than one motion. So the sentence is built around something that keeps almost happening. The closing clause then puts further hardship beyond what has just been described. That refuses the reader any sense of a limit reached.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Descriptions of the hereafter in the Meccan surahs are vivid and short. They address an audience that treated death as a final ending and denied any accounting after it. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars treat the imagery as real and as beyond full grasp in this life. They generally decline to press the physical details past what the words say.

keyTerms.note: A form built for an action done in stages and with difficulty, swallow after swallow. The verb occurs only here in the Quran. Its whole force lies in the effort it makes audible.

keyTerms.gloss: and can hardly get it down
keyTerms.note: The verb means to swallow easily, of a drink that goes down without resistance. The negation with the auxiliary before it makes the act barely possible rather than impossible, which is the point.
The word for something dense and coarse, used of cloth and of hearts as well as of punishment. It names weight rather than sharpness. That is why the rendering relentless catches its sense.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Thirst was the death everyone in that country could picture. Travellers died within a day of it, and herds were lost to it. The sight of a person unable to drink was familiar from illness and from the end of life. The passage does not describe an exotic torment. It takes the most ordinary form of suffering that world knew and removes its ending.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb describing the repeated, difficult swallowing in this ayah occurs only once in the Quran. Arabic has a common verb for drinking and several for gulping. The Book reaches instead for a form meaning to take something down in reluctant instalments. It is a word chosen for the action it makes a listener imagine.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What the passage describes is not more pain but the removal of an ending. That is the exact thing that makes the hereafter hard to picture. Every suffering people know is bounded by exhaustion or by death. This ayah takes both limits away in one sentence. It also keeps the description physical rather than abstract. The Meccan surahs do that again and again, pressing on an audience that thought death settled everything.

crossReferences.why: The drink this ayah describes being swallowed, named in the ayah immediately before.
Uses the same formula about neither dying nor living, of one who comes as a criminal.
The other side of the same passage, where the greeting exchanged is peace.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your ability to bear things rests on knowing they will end: the shift, the illness, the difficult week. Say that out loud once today as an actual observation about yourself. Endings are a mercy you are using constantly, and you have never thanked anyone for them.
studies.explainEasier: In the next life, a person who did wrong tries to drink something awful. He can hardly get it down. Pain comes at him from every side, but he does not die.

studies.title: Ashes On A Stormy Day
studies.meaning: The parable is about a kind of loss rather than about punishment. Ashes are already what remains after something has burned. The image begins with a residue and then removes even that. The wind is violent and the day is stormy, which doubles the force. The point lands in the clause that follows: they have no power over anything they earned. Early scholars stress the word earned. The deeds were real and were done, and the failure is in what they were attached to.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Meccans performed genuine acts of generosity, hospitality and honour, and were proud of them. The Quran repeatedly acknowledges such deeds while denying them a lasting result when they rest on nothing. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars note that the parable addresses good works specifically rather than crimes. That is what makes it disquieting.

keyTerms.note: The word occurs only once in the Quran. Ashes are the end product of a fire, weightless and shapeless. So the comparison starts from something already reduced, before the wind is even mentioned.
The adjective belongs properly to the wind and is attached to the day instead. Arabic uses that construction to spread a quality over a whole span. The entire day is made of storm, not one gust.

The ordinary commercial verb for getting something by effort. It concedes that the deeds were genuinely theirs and genuinely worked for. That is precisely why the image of them scattering is so severe.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every household had a hearth. Everyone knew what happened to a cold fire's ashes when the wind came up: they went completely, leaving the ground clean. There was no gathering them. Fire was made with effort and kept alive on purpose. The sight of a season's hearth scattered in a morning was familiar and slightly desolate.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for ashes occurs only once in the Quran, here. The Book uses a great many images for actions coming to nothing, including scattered dust and a mirage in the desert. Each appears in a different surah. This is the only place ashes are used, and the parable is built so that the wind is almost unnecessary.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates the value of a deed from the doing of it. Good acts done for nothing beyond themselves are described as real, as earned, and as unrecoverable. That puts the whole weight on what a life is aimed at. It is an uncomfortable claim, and the Quran states it as a picture rather than an argument. The reader is left to check their own hearth.

crossReferences.why: The other great parable of wasted works: a mirage a thirsty man crosses a plain to reach.
Describes deeds turned into scattered dust, using a different image for the same outcome.
The opposite case in this same surah: God makes the believers firm with a word that holds.

studies.applyIt: Take one good thing you did this week and ask, plainly, who it was for. Not to disqualify it. Most acts have several reasons inside them, and that is normal. Simply find one that was mostly for something visible, and do the same act again tomorrow with the reason changed.
studies.explainEasier: This is about people who refuse their Lord. Their good deeds are like ashes left after a fire. On a stormy day the wind blows them all away. Nothing is left to hold.

studies.title: He Could Bring A New Creation
studies.meaning: A question is put that assumes its answer, and the assumption is the argument. The heavens and the earth were made with truth, meaning purposefully and rightly, not as decoration or accident. From that comes one consequence. If He wills, He can take you away and bring another creation. The second ayah is four words long in Arabic and does the real work. It removes any suggestion that such a replacement would cost effort. Early scholars note the passage is about whether any people are needed, rather than about power in general.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The families running the city thought themselves permanent. They were guardians of a sanctuary and of a trade nobody else could manage, and the message threatened arrangements they assumed were fixed. No occasion is reported for these ayat. Early scholars note that the same formula appears elsewhere in the Quran, addressed to a community warned that it can be exchanged for another people.

keyTerms.note: The word covers truth, reality and what is due. Creating with it means creating so that things are as they should be, and for a reason. That rules out both randomness and play.
The phrase appears twice in the Quran, both times as a possibility rather than a threat carried out. It is indefinite, so what is imagined is not a better creation but simply another one.
The adjective usually means mighty, but its root also carries scarcity and difficulty. Negated here it means such a thing would not be hard. That is the sense the classical commentaries give it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The desert kept the evidence. Traders passed the remains of peoples who had been permanent in their own estimation and were now a name and a ruin. The Quran points at those places repeatedly. A Meccan hearing that a creation could be replaced without difficulty was not being asked to imagine something. He was being asked to look at the road he took to Syria.
studies.didYouKnow: The short second ayah here contains only four words in Arabic. It works as a comment on the one before it. Very short ayat of this kind, attached to a longer statement to remove a possible objection, are a recognisable feature of the Meccan surahs. This pairing appears again almost word for word in a later surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Purpose and contingency are stated together, and neither cancels the other. Creation is made rightly and for a reason. No particular creature or people is required for that reason to be served. The passage aims at a specific self-image, the assumption that one is necessary, and it removes it gently. What follows in this surah is not destruction but a description of two kinds of people and what becomes of them.

crossReferences.why: Repeats this exact pairing, including the clause that such a replacement is not difficult.
Warns a community that if it turns away, another people will be brought who are not like it.
The parable just before, where works without an anchor scatter like ashes on a windy day.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you believe would fall apart without you: a project, a family arrangement, a group. Now plan for one week off it, actually off it, and let someone else hold it. You will learn something true either way. The ayah's point is not that you do not matter, but that the world is not resting on you.
studies.explainEasier: God made the sky and the earth for a real reason. If he wanted, he could take all people away and make a new creation instead. That would not be hard for him at all.

studies.title: We Were Only Following You
studies.meaning: Everyone comes out into the open together, and the first thing that happens is an argument. The weak turn on those who were proud. They ask them to take a share of the punishment, since they took the share of the following. The answer is not a refusal but a shrug. Had God guided us, we would have guided you. Early scholars note that the exchange contains no denial of the relationship. What collapses is the assumption that a follower's account can be settled by whoever they followed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The city's structure ran on clientage. Weaker men attached themselves to stronger houses for protection and took their positions from them, including on the question of the new message. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars note that the same scene of followers and leaders arguing recurs across several surahs. It always has the same outcome, and the leaders never offer anything.

keyTerms.note: A verb for coming out into open ground where nothing is hidden. It occurs twice in the Quran, and both are in this surah. The surah uses it to open and close its account of that day.

A collective noun rather than a plural, so it describes them as a body rather than as individuals. That is precisely the identity the ayah dissolves, since the answer they receive addresses no body at all.
From a root meaning to swerve aside from something. It names not a hiding place but a way of turning off the road. That is what both parties want, and what the sentence denies them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A client in Mecca owed his patron loyalty and received protection in return. The arrangement covered opinions as well as safety. Which gods a man honoured, which disputes he entered and whose side he took were largely settled by whose house he belonged to. The ayah addresses people for whom following was not weakness of character but the ordinary structure of a life.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for coming out into the open before God occurs twice in the Quran. Both are in this surah, at this scene and again near its end. The two uses bracket a long passage. So the same image opens and closes the surah's account of that day, with everything else set between them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Responsibility is shown as something that cannot be handed on, and the passage makes the point through a conversation rather than a rule. Neither party disputes what happened. They dispute whether it can be shared out, and the answer is that it cannot. The leaders' reply is instructive too. They plead their own lack of guidance, which concedes that they were never in a position to be relied on.

crossReferences.why: The same verb for emerging before God, used again at the close of this surah's account.
The next speech in the same scene, where blame is refused once more and returned to them.
The fullest version of this argument between the weak and the arrogant, at greater length.

studies.applyIt: Find one position you hold mainly because the people around you hold it. Not a wrong one necessarily; just one you have never examined on its own. Spend half an hour with the best case against it. You may end up where you started, and it will be yours rather than borrowed.
studies.explainEasier: On that day everyone stands out in the open. The weak people ask their old leaders to take some of their punishment. The leaders say no. They had no guidance to give in the first place.

studies.title: I Had No Power Over You
studies.meaning: The speech comes after the matter is settled, which is why it can afford to be honest. God's promise was true and mine was not. I had no authority over you. I called, and you answered. Then the sentence readers remember: do not blame me, blame yourselves. Early scholars note that the whole account of temptation is reduced here to an invitation. The response was supplied entirely by the person who accepted it. The speech ends by disowning the people who had associated him with God.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to a society that took unseen powers seriously and treated them as forces to be managed with offerings and ritual. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars note that this is one of the few passages where the enemy of humanity is given a long speech. Everything he says in it is treated as true. He speaks at a point where deception no longer serves him.

keyTerms.note: The same phrase Joseph used in an Egyptian prison to close a reading of two dreams. Here it marks the point past which nothing can be revised. That is why the speech that follows is candid.
A sanction that entitles or compels. Denying he had any of it reduces his whole activity to a call. The Quran uses the same word elsewhere for the warrant idols were said to lack.
From a root for shouting for rescue. The word appears twice in this one ayah, once denied of him and once denied of them. The two parties are refused each other in the same breath.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The relationship this speech dissolves was a familiar one. A man attached himself to a stronger party and expected to be answered when he called. That was what protection meant, and calls for help were made aloud and in public. Everyone listening had shouted for someone once. The ayah describes two parties discovering, at the same moment, that neither will come.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for one who answers a cry for rescue occurs twice in the Quran. Both times are in this single ayah, once denied by him of himself and once denied of his followers. The Book reaches for a rare term and then uses it twice in one sentence. That is how the mutual abandonment is made audible.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage gives temptation its exact size. There was a call, and there was an answer, and the answer belonged entirely to the one who gave it. That removes two excuses at once. One is the person who blames an outside force, the other the person who imagines that force can be bargained with. It also leaves the reader with a strange source for the clearest statement of human responsibility in the surah.

crossReferences.why: The same phrase about a settled matter, spoken by Joseph in prison to two fellow inmates.
The same figure claiming he will mislead, and being told he has no power over God's servants.
The argument immediately before, where followers try to hand their share to their leaders.

studies.applyIt: Take one habit you describe as something that comes over you. Rewrite the sentence today with yourself as the subject: not it takes hold of me, but I answer it. Say it that way for a week. The change is grammatical, and it moves the thing from weather to a decision you are making.
studies.explainEasier: After everything is decided, Satan speaks. He says God kept his promise and he did not. He had no power over anyone. He only called, and people chose to come. He tells them to blame themselves.

studies.title: Their Greeting There Is Peace
studies.meaning: After several ayat of argument and blame, this one is quiet. Those who believed and did good are admitted. The Quran almost always keeps those two conditions together. The entry is by their Lord's leave, which repeats the qualification in the surah's opening ayah. Then comes the last clause: their greeting in it is peace. That is the whole reason for placing this ayah here. Early scholars note that the scene just before was two groups blaming each other. What is named here is the end of that.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The greeting named here was already the ordinary Arabian greeting, exchanged at doors and on roads. It was withheld from people a community had broken with. Members of the early Muslim community were being denied it in Mecca. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars note the contrast the surah builds between this scene and the argument just before it.

keyTerms.note: The same qualification used in this surah's first ayah about bringing people out of darkness. Entry to the garden is described the way guidance was: real, and not achieved by the one entering alone.
A participle for continuing without end. The Quran uses it of both destinations, so it is a word about duration rather than about reward. That is what makes the previous ayat as heavy as they are.
The word for greeting comes from the root for life, since the greeting it names was originally a wish for long life. Here it is replaced by peace. The scene just before had none of that.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A greeting was a social act with consequences. Returning it acknowledged a person. Withholding it announced a breach that everyone present could see. Members of a boycotted family were passed in silence in the streets of their own city. The promise that a greeting will be exchanged, and that the greeting will be peace, spoke directly to people who were being walked past.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for their greeting comes from the same root as the word for life. The pre-Islamic greeting it replaced was a wish that the person live long. The Quran keeps the old noun and changes what is said. So a greeting about staying alive becomes one about being at peace.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The garden is described not by its pleasures but by its speech. What is named as typical of it is a greeting. That is a claim about relations between people rather than about scenery. Set against an argument where each party tried to hand its burden to the other, the ayah defines the destination as the place where that conversation is over. It is also the shortest clause in the passage.

crossReferences.why: The argument this ayah answers, where the weak and the proud blame each other.
Uses the same word for greeting, and names their closing call as praise to the Lord of the worlds.
Describes the garden as free of idle and sinful talk, with only the saying of peace.

studies.applyIt: Greet someone properly today whom you usually pass with a nod: a neighbour, a colleague on another floor, the person at the till. Full words, eye contact, a second of pause. The ayah names a greeting as the typical act of the best place there is. That is worth taking literally once.
studies.explainEasier: People who believed and did good are let into gardens with rivers flowing under them. God lets them in. They stay there for good. When they meet, the word they say to each other is peace.

studies.title: The Tree With Firm Roots
studies.meaning: The comparison is offered to be looked at, not argued over. A good word is like a good tree. Its root is fixed in the ground. Its branches reach upward. It gives fruit in every season by its Lord's leave. Early scholars most often take the good word to be the declaration of faith. Some read it more widely, as any true and useful speech. Two ayat later the contrast arrives: a bad tree with nothing holding it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is named for Abraham and is built around the difference between what lasts and what falls apart. The parable comes straight after a scene of the Day of Judgement. In it, followers turn on the ones they followed, and Satan denies that he is answerable for them. Putting an image of deep roots right after that collapse is deliberate. Early sources report no particular occasion for the parable.

keyTerms.note: The adjective covers what is clean, pleasant and fit for use, and it is applied to food, land, speech and people. It is a word of quality rather than of correctness, so a good word is one that nourishes.
The same noun means the foundation of a building, the principle behind an argument, and a person's lineage. What is being praised is not the visible tree but the part nobody sees.
An active participle of a verb meaning to stand fast and not be moved. Three ayat later the same root describes what God gives believers in this life and the next, which links the tree to the person.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A date palm was the closest thing to a bank in that world. It took years to bear, outlived the person who planted it, and produced through drought because its roots reached water that surface crops could not. Families were known by their groves, and a palm cut down in a raid was a wound that lasted a generation. Everyone hearing this knew what a tree with a firm root was worth.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran does not name the tree. A well-known report from the companions calls it the date palm, and many early scholars follow that. Others leave it open, on the grounds that the parable works better with no species attached. The parable is also unusual in giving both halves, a good tree and a bad one, within three ayat.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Faith is described as a thing with structure. It has a hidden part that holds it and a visible part that bears. The parable insists the second rests entirely on the first. That changes what counts as religious progress. Growing upward is not the achievement, since a tree can be tall and still come out of the ground. The fruit is said to come by leave, so even the visible result is not simply owned by the one bearing it.

crossReferences.why: Completes the parable with the uprooted tree and applies it to firmness given in both lives.
Traces the upward movement of good speech and righteous action to God.
Sorts truth from falsehood by what stays in the ground rather than what rises to view.

studies.applyIt: Notice one sentence you say often to someone you live with. It might be a complaint, a joke, a piece of praise, or nothing much at all. Ask yourself what it has been planting in them over the last year. Then choose one better sentence and say it today, and again tomorrow, without explaining why you are saying it.
studies.explainEasier: God gives a picture here. A good word is like a good tree. Its roots are firm in the ground and its branches reach up into the sky. A tree like that keeps giving fruit.

studies.title: Fruit In Every Season
studies.meaning: The point of these two ayat is the tree's yield, not its shape. It gives its fruit every season. The phrase can be read as at all times or at each appointed time, and early scholars allow both. A qualification follows at once, by its Lord's leave. It keeps the fruiting from being a property of the tree. Then the contrast. A bad word is a bad tree, torn up from the ground, with no place to stand. The second image has no root at all rather than a weak one.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, spoken in a country where a productive tree was a form of wealth and a dead one was firewood. No occasion is reported for these ayat. Early scholars record several readings of what the good word and the good tree refer to. The declaration of God's oneness and the date palm are most often named. They treat the parable as open enough to cover a person's whole speech and life.

keyTerms.note: The noun means an unspecified stretch of time. Early scholars read it as constantly, or as at each due time. The ambiguity is useful: the tree either never stops or always delivers when it should.
A passive verb for uprooting something completely, pulled from the surface rather than dug out. It suggests the tree came away easily. That is the difference between the two images.
From the root for staying put. The word covers a resting place and the condition of being settled at once. So the bad tree lacks both a location and the quality of remaining anywhere.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A date palm was a family's capital. It took years to come into bearing, produced for generations, and gave fruit, timber, rope, matting and shade. Farmers reckoned wealth in trees rather than in coins. A shrub uprooted by hand from thin soil was the opposite kind of plant: no investment, no yield, and nothing lost when the wind took it away.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing when the good tree yields is open in its grammar. The classical commentaries preserve a range of readings for it, from every moment to each appointed season. Some early authorities connected it to the date harvest, and others read it as continuous. The tradition kept the alternatives rather than settling on one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The parable measures words by what they keep producing rather than by how they sound. A good word yields over time, and it does so by permission. That places even a person's best speech inside a dependence rather than an achievement. The bad word is not answered with an argument at all. It is simply described as having nowhere to stand, which is a claim about durability rather than about immediate effect.

crossReferences.why: The first half of the parable, where the good tree's root is firm and its branches high.
Applies the image to people: God makes those who believe firm with the word that holds.
Another parable of what lasts and what is carried off, using water and a rising scum.

studies.applyIt: Think of something true you said years ago that is still working in someone: a piece of advice, a word of encouragement, a correction offered kindly. You will probably have to be told about it rather than knowing. Say one more of those this week, and let yourself never find out what it does.
studies.explainEasier: A good word is like a good tree. It gives fruit in every season, because God lets it. A bad word is like a bad tree. It is pulled out of the ground and has nowhere to stand.

studies.title: The Word That Holds
studies.meaning: The parable is applied to people, and the verb chosen is the one the tree image was built on. God makes them firm. What does the holding is a word, described with the same adjective used of the good tree's root. Two locations are named, this life and the hereafter. The classical tradition connects the second to the questioning that follows death. The ayah then states the other side in three short clauses. It ends on a sentence that refuses any further explanation: God does what He wills.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Members of the community were being pressed to take back what they had said, sometimes under physical force. Firmness under questioning was a live and practical concern rather than an abstraction. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Classical commentary connects the reference to the hereafter with reports about the questioning of a person after burial. It treats the ayah as covering both settings together.

keyTerms.note: A causative from the root for standing fast, the same root used of the good tree's root in the parable. Firmness is described as something done to a person rather than mustered by them.
The phrase occurs only here in the Quran. It carries the parable across from trees to speech. So what steadies a person under pressure is something they have said and can say again.

keyTerms.gloss: and God does what He wills
keyTerms.note: A closing formula that declines to give further account. The Quran uses it where a statement about guidance might otherwise invite a demand for reasons. It stops the sentence rather than completing an argument.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man's word was the only instrument he had in a dispute. Oaths were sworn aloud, and agreements held because they had been said in front of people. A person who could be made to take back what he had said lost everything that followed from it. Firmness in speech was not a private virtue in that world. It was the whole of a man's standing.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for the word that stands firm occurs only once in the Quran, here. Its adjective is the same one used three ayat earlier for the good tree's root. One Arabic word connects two things. It joins a tree that cannot be pulled up to a person who cannot be talked out of what they said.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Steadfastness is described as given rather than generated, which changes what a person can reasonably do about it. What they hold is a word. Words are said, repeated and kept in use, so the passage points towards practice rather than towards effort of will. The closing clause then removes the temptation to treat the arrangement as a machine. It leaves guidance where the surah has kept it throughout.

crossReferences.why: The parable this ayah applies, where the good tree's root is described as firm.
The opposite case in this surah: works with no anchor, scattered like ashes in a storm.
The prayer that follows from this: do not let our hearts swerve after You have guided us.

studies.applyIt: Choose one short sentence of your faith and say it deliberately once a day this week, out loud, at the same moment. Not as a charm. This ayah describes people being held firm by a word. A word you have not said in a year is not available to you when you need it.
studies.explainEasier: God keeps believers steady with a word that holds. He does that in this life and after death too. People who do wrong are left to wander. God does whatever he wants.

studies.title: They Exchanged The Blessing
studies.meaning: The charge is put as a trade. A blessing was received and swapped for ingratitude. The trade took a whole people down with those who made it. Early scholars discuss what the blessing was, and most name the coming of a messenger to them. They note that the leaders are described as landing their people somewhere rather than merely misleading them. Then the last of the three ayat turns to address them directly, with a permission that is not one: enjoy yourselves, your destination is the Fire.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Early scholars identify the people described here in more than one way. Some connect the passage to the leaders of Quraysh, who had received a messenger from among themselves. The surah's setting supports that reading without requiring it. No specific occasion is reported. The final instruction to enjoy themselves is a form the Quran uses elsewhere for a warning delivered as an invitation.

keyTerms.note: A commercial verb for putting one thing in place of another. It makes ingratitude an active trade rather than a lapse, and it implies they received something in return that they judged worth having.
The second word means perishing, and also goods that will not sell, left on a merchant's hands. The phrase occurs only here, and it keeps the commercial image of the exchange running.
Things treated as comparable to God. The word is about parity rather than worship. So the charge is a category error before it is an act. The Quran uses it for anything given equal weight.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan leaders decided for their people. A clan chief's ruling bound his household and his clients. Those who followed had little real choice about the direction taken. The ayah says the leaders landed their people somewhere. That is the language of a caravan master, who brings a party to a halt at a chosen place. It is exactly how that power was felt.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for the house of ruin occurs only here in the Quran. Its second word doubles as the merchant's term for stock that will not sell.
