The whole passage is built from trade vocabulary: something exchanged, a destination arrived at, and goods left worthless. It is addressed to a city that lived by commerce.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ingratitude is described as an exchange rather than an absence, which means something was accepted in return. That makes rejection a purchase a person made and can be asked about. The passage also insists that such decisions are not private. Those who made this trade are said to have brought a whole people with them. That is the Quran's usual view of what leadership does with its errors.

crossReferences.why: The declaration this passage inverts: thanks brings increase, and ingratitude meets severity.
Names the blessings that cannot be counted, and the human being as unjust and ungrateful.
Uses the same word for rivals set up beside God, immediately after listing what He provides.

studies.applyIt: Pick one good thing in your life that you complained about this month. Say what you actually traded it for in that moment. It might be a bit of sympathy, the pleasure of being heard, or a reason not to try. Naming the return you took is more useful than resolving to complain less.
studies.explainEasier: Some people were given something good from God. Instead of thanking him, they swapped it away. Their leaders took the whole people down with them. They are told to enjoy themselves for now. In the end their home is the Fire.

studies.title: Before A Day Of No Bargaining
studies.meaning: The address changes and softens. Tell My servants who have believed, God says, and the possessive is doing work after three ayat about people who set up rivals. Two practices are named together: the prayer kept up, and giving from what has been provided. The giving is to be done both privately and openly. Then comes a deadline, described by what it lacks: a day with no trading in it and no friendship. Early scholars note that both named exemptions are the ordinary ways a debt gets settled between people.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Mecca ran on exactly the two things this day is said to be without: trade, and the network of friendship and clientage that let a man call in a favour when he was short. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars note the gentleness of the address, coming immediately after a passage of warning. They read the shift as deliberate.

keyTerms.note: The possessive is unusual and pointed. After three ayat about people who set up rivals, the believers are named as belonging to God. The message is passed to them rather than at them.
Both are named without one being ranked above the other. Private giving protects the receiver's dignity and the giver's sincerity. Open giving makes the practice visible, and the ayah asks for both.
The second word means close friendship of the kind that carries obligations. The phrase occurs only here. It closes the two doors by which anything ever got settled late in that society.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A Meccan short of what he owed had two options, and everyone knew them: sell something, or go to a friend. Trade and friendship were the two instruments of settlement. A man's whole security lay in having access to both. Naming a day on which neither exists was not a poetic image. It described the removal of the only two exits an audience of merchants had ever used.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of trade and friendship as the two things absent on that day occurs only here in the Quran. A related passage in an earlier surah names three absent things instead. It adds speaking up for someone before God to the list. Both are addressed to people who are being asked to give before a deadline they cannot renegotiate.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two practices are placed side by side as one instruction, one directed upwards and one outwards. The passage does not separate them. The deadline given for both is defined by the collapse of every human means of settling an account. That puts what a person does now beyond the reach of later repair. The address as My servants keeps this from being a threat, since the whole instruction is entrusted to people who already belong.

crossReferences.why: The parallel warning, naming a day with no trading, no friendship and no speaking up for anyone.
Describes those who spend by night and day, secretly and openly, in almost these words.
Lists what has been provided, immediately after the instruction to give from it.

studies.applyIt: Give something small today without telling anyone, and give something small this week where people can see it. The ayah names both and ranks neither. Doing the pair in one week tends to show you which of the two you have been avoiding, and why.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the people who believe to keep up their prayer. He tells them to give from what he gave them, in secret and openly. One day no one can buy help or ask a friend for it.

studies.title: The Ships And The Rivers
studies.meaning: A list begins, and one verb governs most of it. Things are described as put at your service, made to run for you. That is a different claim from saying they were made. Water comes down, fruit comes up, ships cross a sea by His command, rivers are set to run. Early scholars note that two of the four items are human inventions or human uses. So the passage credits God with the workability of the world rather than only with its contents.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to a trading city whose wealth depended on sea routes through the Red Sea and on caravans supplied by rivers and wells further north. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars note that the list is offered in the middle of a warning passage. They read it as evidence produced rather than as consolation. The argument turns on whether the audience will see where these arrangements come from.

keyTerms.gloss: and He put at your service
keyTerms.note: The verb means to make something work for another without payment. It appears four times across this ayah and the next. It is more concentrated here than anywhere else in the Quran.
Attached specifically to the ships. Sailing depends on wind and current, which no crew controls. So the qualification is placed exactly where a sailor knows his own competence runs out.
The word for what sustains a creature, always in the Quran something given rather than obtained. Placing it after rain and fruit names the whole sequence as one act of provision.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccans knew ships from the Red Sea ports and from the grain that came up from Egypt. They knew rivers by their absence at home and their presence on the roads north. A ship crossing water it should sink into was one of the standard wonders traders talked about. The list in this ayah describes the routes by which their city was fed.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for putting something at human service occurs four times in this ayah and the one after it. Four uses fall within two neighbouring ayat. That is the densest concentration of the word anywhere in the Quran. The items it governs move outward in scale, from ships and rivers to the sun, the moon, and the night and day.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage argues from usability rather than from grandeur. What is offered as evidence is not that the world is vast, but that it works for creatures who did not arrange it. Water arrives, seeds respond, the sea holds a hull up. That is an argument a person can check from inside an ordinary day. It places provision, not power, at the centre of what these signs are said to show.

crossReferences.why: Continues the same list with the sun, the moon, and the alternation of night and day.
Closes the sequence by saying these blessings cannot be counted, and naming the human response.
Repeats the image of ships cutting through the sea, alongside what is drawn out of it.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you used today that only works because something enormous stays reliable: a tap, a bus timetable, bread. Trace it back three steps out loud, to rain or to the sun. Stop there. The point is not to arrive at a conclusion but to notice how few steps it takes.
studies.explainEasier: God sends rain down from the sky, and fruit grows for you to eat. He makes ships sail on the sea and rivers run on the land. All of it is put to work for people.

studies.title: Both Pursuing Their Courses
studies.meaning: Two more items are added to the list, and the second pair is the surprising one. The sun and the moon are described with a word meaning tireless persistence, running without pause. Then night and day themselves are named as put at human service. Early scholars note the move: time is treated as a provision rather than as a container. The alternation lets a person work and then stop, and know where they are in a month. It is presented as an arrangement made for creatures who need one.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to people who navigated by stars, timed caravans by the moon and organised the year by lunar months. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars note that the heavenly bodies here are described as serving rather than as being served. That contrasts sharply with the surrounding religious culture, where the sun and moon were among the objects that received honour.

keyTerms.note: A dual participle from the root for keeping at something without slackening. The same root described the farming Joseph prescribed for seven unbroken years. So one word covers a nation's labour and the heavens' motion.
Named as items put at human service, alongside physical things. Time is not treated here as a background but as something arranged. That is why the ayah can list it with rivers and ships.
Repeated twice more in this short ayah. The Quran often builds an argument by repetition rather than by connectives. The recurring verb is what holds this list together across two ayat.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything was timed by the sky. Travel began before dawn and stopped at the heat. Caravans moved by moonlight when the sand was cool. Debts fell due at a named moon, and the pilgrimage season was fixed the same way. A merchant could read the month from a glance at the sky. A night's brightness decided whether a party moved or camped.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the sun and moon as tirelessly persisting comes from one root. The same root gives the term used two surahs earlier, where Joseph tells Egypt to farm steadily for seven unbroken years. One word for unresting regularity covers a nation's farming and the movement of the heavens.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming night and day as things placed at human service says something specific about time. It is not merely the setting in which life happens. It is part of the provision, arranged so that a creature who cannot work without stopping has an alternation built for it. That makes rest a gift rather than a concession. It also puts the sun and the moon in the position of servants, in a culture that had treated them otherwise.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same root for unbroken persistence, of seven consecutive years of farming.
Names sleep as rest, night as covering and day as a means of livelihood, in three short ayat.
The first half of this list, where water, fruit, ships and rivers are named.

studies.applyIt: Go to bed tonight treating the night as something provided rather than as what is left over. That means stopping while there is still work, on purpose, once. Notice how strongly you want to finish the thing first. The ayah puts night on the same list as bread and rivers.
studies.explainEasier: God made the sun and the moon keep moving without ever stopping. He also made the night and the day work for people. Time itself is one of the good things he gives us.

studies.title: More Than You Can Count
studies.meaning: Two claims and a verdict. God has given something of everything that was asked for. Early scholars read that closely. It is not everything a person asked, but a share from every kind of thing a person might ask. Then the blessings are declared beyond counting. That shuts off any hope of ever settling the account. The last clause calls the human being deeply unjust and stubbornly ungrateful. The strong forms make both traits a habit, not a slip.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah closes a run of verses listing what has been placed at human disposal: rain and the fruit it raises, ships that cross the sea, rivers, the sun and moon in their courses, night and day. Only after that list does the verdict fall. No specific occasion is reported. The surah dates from the difficult later Meccan years, addressed to people who had reason to feel that little had been given.

keyTerms.note: The verb comes from the word for pebbles, which is how counting was done: one stone laid down per item. The image is of a tally that runs out of stones, not of a mind that loses interest.
An intensive form of the word for wrongdoing, whose root means to put something where it does not belong. The charge is not cruelty but misplacement: crediting a gift to the wrong source.
Another intensive, from the root meaning to cover. It describes someone who habitually buries what he has received, and the grammar makes it a settled disposition rather than a single failure.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Counting was physical work. Merchants in Mecca kept accounts with pebbles, knots and memory, and a caravan's profit was reckoned bale by bale on arrival. Herders counted animals through a gate at dusk, every night, because a missing head meant a search before dark. The claim that a tally could not be completed was not a poetic flourish to that audience. It described a specific and familiar failure.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence about blessings beyond counting appears twice in the Quran, here and once more later on. Each time a different clause follows it. In the other place, the follow-on is that God is forgiving and merciful. Here it is that the human being is unjust and ungrateful. Repeating a line with a switched ending is a known feature of the Quran's style.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets something endless against something small, and softens neither. The gifts run past counting, so thanks can never be finished. It is never a debt paid off. Human ingratitude is stated as a standing condition, not as a charge aimed at certain people. Taken together, these leave the bond lopsided for good. That is the point. What comes next in the surah is not a settling of accounts. It is Abraham asking.

crossReferences.why: The other occurrence of the uncountable-blessings sentence, closing on forgiveness instead.
States the promise this ayah measures: thanks bring increase, and the increase is unlimited.
Repeats a single question about denied favours thirty-one times across one surah.

studies.applyIt: Try to count. Sit for two minutes and list, on paper, the blessings of the last hour only: light, a working tap, a body that got you to the chair, someone who is alive. Stop when the two minutes end, not when you run out. The exercise is designed to fail, and noticing where you stopped is the whole of it.
studies.explainEasier: God has given you some of everything you asked for. If you tried to count all the good things he has given, you could never finish the list. Still, people are unfair and forget to say thank you.

studies.title: Keep Me From The Idols
studies.meaning: Abraham asks for two things, and the second is startling in his mouth. Make this land safe, and keep me and my sons from worshipping idols. A man who broke idols when young asks to be kept from them in old age. Early scholars dwell on that as the mark of a man who does not consider himself finished. The second ayah divides people by their relation to him, and stops halfway. Whoever follows me belongs with me, and whoever disobeys me, You are Forgiving and Merciful.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the land Abraham names is the valley in which the audience was living. The surah takes its name from him, although he appears in only these few ayat. No occasion is reported for this passage. Early scholars note the force of the prayer for a city whose people had filled that same sanctuary with images. They note that the prayer for safety is recorded elsewhere in the Quran in slightly different words.

keyTerms.note: From the root behind faith and trust. What he asks for the city first is not wealth or greatness but security. In that country that meant a place where a man could arrive without being killed for his goods.
A causative meaning to set someone off to the side of a thing. He does not ask for strength to resist idols, but to be kept away from them. That is a request about circumstances rather than resolve.
The sentence about those who disobey has no main clause of its own. Instead of naming their fate, he names two of God's attributes. That leaves the outcome with God rather than with him.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The valley Abraham names had no farmland and no river. Its entire economy rested on being a place where fighting was suspended and traders could meet. Safety was the city's product. Everyone hearing this prayer lived on the arrangement it asks for. They had also filled the sanctuary at its centre with exactly what the second half of the prayer asks to be kept from.
studies.didYouKnow: Surah 14 carries Abraham's name and mentions him by name only once, in this passage. The section given to him is a sequence of prayers rather than a story. No episode from his life is told. What the surah preserves of him is the way he asked for things.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer asks to be kept safe from wrongdoing. It does not treat that safety as won. And it comes from a man the Quran presents as unusually firm. That pairing is the point. Being firm does not make a person sure of himself. The half-finished sentence about those who disobey is just as deliberate. Abraham will not pass sentence on people who reject his way. He hands the matter to two names about mercy.

crossReferences.why: The same prayer for the city's safety, recorded with a request for provision attached.
The next prayer in the sequence, about the family he has settled in that valley.
Another figure at a high point declining to declare himself safe from his own soul.

studies.applyIt: Ask to be kept away from something rather than to be strong enough for it, once, this week. Name the actual situation you would like removed from your path. Most of us pray for strength, because asking to be spared feels like an admission. Abraham makes it the request itself.
studies.explainEasier: Abraham prays for this city to be safe. He asks God to keep him and his sons away from idols. Anyone who follows him is one of his own. For anyone who does not, he leaves it to God's mercy.

studies.title: A Valley With Nothing Growing
studies.meaning: The prayer states the situation before it asks for anything, and the statement is bleak. I have settled some of my offspring in a valley with no crops. Then comes the purpose, which is the only reason offered for choosing such a place: so that they may keep up the prayer. Only after that come the two requests, and their order is worth noticing. Hearts first, then fruit. Early scholars observe that he asks for people to be drawn there before he asks for anything to eat.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The valley described is the one the audience lived in. Its barrenness was a plain fact rather than an image, since Mecca grew nothing and imported its food. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars connect the prayer with the settling of Abraham's family at the sanctuary. They note that the city's later wealth came from pilgrimage and trade rather than from farming, which is what the prayer actually asked for.

keyTerms.note: Literally not possessed of sown crops. The phrase occurs only here in the Quran and is entirely factual. There is no soil worth planting and no water to plant with, so nobody can be fed there.
The word for hearts here suggests the burning, eager kind rather than the seat of belief. He asks for people's longing to be turned that way. That is how a barren valley gets fed.
A verb for falling or swooping down towards something, used of birds coming down. It is a strong word. So what is asked for is not mild interest but a pull people act on.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca had no farmland at all. Grain came from Yemen and Syria, dates from Taif, and the city's whole living came from the traffic drawn by the sanctuary and by the trading seasons around it. Every listener knew their bread had travelled. The prayer in this ayah describes the exact arrangement by which they were fed. It was made before there was a city there.
studies.didYouKnow: The prayer asks for hearts to lean towards the valley before it asks for fruit, and the order matches what happened. The city that grew there never became a farming town. It lived on the pilgrimage and the trade that came with it. What fed it was the first request. The fruit arrived on the backs of animals belonging to people who had come.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage shows a request that names an apparently unworkable situation without complaint. The reason given for it has nothing to do with whether the place could support anyone. Prayer was the purpose. The food came second in the asking and second in the arriving. It also shows provision arriving through people rather than from the ground. That widens what a person may reasonably ask for when their own circumstances have no local solution.

crossReferences.why: The prayer immediately before, asking for the same city's safety and for distance from idols.
The same request recorded elsewhere, pairing the city's security with provision of fruits.
Describes the city fed and secured through the trading journeys that answered this prayer.

studies.applyIt: Ask for something this week whose route you cannot see. Not a vague good outcome, but a specific thing, in a situation where you genuinely do not know how it could arrive. Say the situation plainly first, the way this prayer does, and then ask anyway.
studies.explainEasier: Abraham left part of his family in a valley where nothing grows. He did it so they would pray there. He asks God to make people want to come, and to give them fruit to eat.

studies.title: Given Sons In Old Age
studies.meaning: Between two requests he stops asking and says two other things. First, that God knows what is hidden and what is said aloud. That admits there is more in the prayer than the words carry. Then praise, and the reason for it is domestic: two sons given to an old man. He names both. Early scholars note that the thanks comes in the middle of a sequence of requests, not at the end. It closes by calling God the Hearer of prayer, which is what the surrounding requests depend on.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience traced its descent through one of the two sons named here. The other stood at the head of the community that had received earlier scripture. So the ayah names in one breath the ancestry of the people listening and of their neighbours. No occasion is reported for these ayat. Early scholars treat the passage as part of a single continuous prayer.

keyTerms.note: A pair covering everything a person might carry. Saying it inside a prayer concedes that the words being spoken are not the whole request. It asks for the rest to be counted too.
The preposition carries the sense of upon or against, so the gift is described as arriving over the top of the obstacle. He names the difficulty in the same clause as the thanks.
Not simply one who hears, but one who hears prayer in particular. The name is arrived at here as a conclusion drawn from what he has already been given, rather than as a doctrine stated.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Children were a household's whole security. Sons worked the herds, defended the camp, carried a man's name and cared for him when he could no longer travel. A childless old man had nobody obliged to him and no future in the world. Naming two sons received late was therefore not sentiment. It named the difference between a line that ended and one that continued.
studies.didYouKnow: The two sons named in this prayer stand at the head of two peoples. The Arabs traced their descent through one, and the Children of Israel through the other. Abraham names them together in a single sentence of thanks. The Quran preserves the pairing without comment, in a passage that is otherwise entirely a prayer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Praise is placed in the middle of asking rather than after it, which changes the shape of the whole prayer. What he thanks for is also his evidence. It is a specific thing already given, from which he draws a conclusion about God being one who hears. The admission about what is hidden is equally practical. It lets a person pray honestly without being able to put everything they carry into words.

crossReferences.why: The request just before this pause, about the family settled in a barren valley.
The prayers that follow, moving from his household to the whole community of believers.
Another prayer for a child in old age, answered, and using the same name for God who hears.

studies.applyIt: Put one line of thanks in the middle of your next request rather than at the end. Make it about something already given that is the same kind of thing you are asking for. It changes the asking. You end up petitioning from evidence rather than from need alone.
studies.explainEasier: Abraham says that God knows what we keep quiet and what we say out loud. Then he stops asking and says thank you. God gave him two sons when he was already old. God hears prayers.

studies.title: A Prayer For The Reckoning
studies.meaning: Two requests end a long prayer. The first does not ask for prayer itself. It asks to be made someone who keeps prayer standing. That is a request about character, not about an act. It reaches his children too, without taking them for granted. The second request opens wider: forgiveness for himself, for his parents, and for all believers on the day the account stands. Early scholars note that the request for the parents belongs to a stage before it was clear his father would not turn.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah carries Abraham's name and closes its middle section with a sequence of his prayers, spoken after settling part of his family in the barren valley beside the Sacred House. The Meccan audience traced its lineage and its sanctuary to him, so hearing his prayers quoted was hearing their own founder ask for exactly what they were refusing. No specific occasion is reported for these two ayat.

keyTerms.note: An active participle from the verb to make something stand upright. Applied to prayer it means keeping it standing rather than merely performing it, which is why the request is for a kind of person.
A form built on the verb to receive, intensified. It asks not that the prayer be heard but that it be taken and approved, which assumes hearing and worries about the step after it.

An ordinary commercial word for settling a ledger. The day is described by the verb to stand, as if the accounting itself rises to its feet, which is closer to a court convening than to a scene of terror.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An old man's prayers for his line were not sentimental in that world. Descent was the whole of a person's safety. A family with no sons in the next generation simply vanished. Its wells and its name were taken up by neighbours. Abraham asks for something a family tree cannot secure. The people hearing it could recite their descent from him for twenty generations. They could still be the very thing the prayer asked not to happen.
studies.didYouKnow: Abraham's prayers run through seven ayat in a row here. That is one of the longest unbroken prayers given to a single figure in the Quran. The surah is one of only six named after a prophet. It is also one of the few places where a prophet prays for believers in general rather than for his own people. That widening arrives in the very last clause.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer shows what a settled bond with God sounds like from the inside. Abraham does not ask to be spared the reckoning. He asks to be forgiven at it, which accepts the whole arrangement. He asks about character rather than outcomes. The last thing he asks for is not for himself. Putting this in the mouth of the figure his hearers honoured most makes humility before judgement look like the grown form of faith, not the frightened one.

crossReferences.why: The rest of the same supplication, from the request for a safe city to thanks for two sons in old age.
Explains why Abraham asked forgiveness for his father, and why he stopped.
Gives the prayer for parents in its most quoted form, joined to mercy in childhood.

studies.applyIt: Say a prayer today that includes someone you have never met. Abraham's last clause reaches past his family to all believers, and prayer is one of the few things you can give a stranger without their knowing. Name a category out loud: people in hospital tonight, people burying someone this week. Thirty seconds is enough.
studies.explainEasier: Abraham asks God to make him a person who keeps up prayer, and his children too. He asks God to accept his prayer. He asks God to forgive him, his parents, and everyone who believes.

studies.title: He Only Defers Them
studies.meaning: The instruction is addressed to the observer rather than to the wrongdoer. Do not ever suppose that God is unaware of what they are doing. What looks like inattention is named as postponement, and the delay has a date attached. Then the second ayah describes their posture on that day in four short strokes: necks stretched, heads raised, eyes not blinking, hearts empty. Early scholars note that every detail concerns the body except the last. The last is what the description is for.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, when the community had watched injustice go unanswered for years and had no way to get redress. No occasion is reported for these ayat. Early scholars note that the prohibition is emphatic in the grammar. So what is ruled out is not merely a conclusion but the drift of thought that produces it. That drift is the natural response of anyone watching wrongdoing prosper for a long time.

keyTerms.note: An emphatic prohibition against reckoning something to be the case. It addresses a calculation rather than a belief. That is why the ayah aims at an observer's conclusion instead of at a doctrine.

keyTerms.gloss: on which the eyes fix, staring
keyTerms.note: The verb describes an eye that has stopped moving and will not close. It occurs only here in the Quran. It names the sign of a person unable to look away from what they see.
The word means empty air, the space in a hollow thing. Three details are physical; the last is interior. That is why the phrase has stayed memorable.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everyone in that world had seen a strong man do what he liked and die comfortable. Blood money was paid or not paid according to who could enforce it, and a weak clan absorbed injuries it could not answer. Telling such an audience that God was not inattentive addressed a real and specific grievance. It was not a general reassurance about how the world is run.
studies.didYouKnow: The emphatic prohibition that opens this ayah returns five ayat later, at the start of another warning in the same passage. So the section is bracketed by the same words, used twice. The Quran uses this construction sparingly, and two of its occurrences fall within six ayat of each other here.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Delay is distinguished from indifference. The distinction is offered as something to hold, not as an explanation of why the delay happens. No reason for the postponement is given at all. What the passage supplies instead is a description of the endpoint, detailed enough to be believed. That is how the Quran usually answers the complaint that wrongdoing is not being addressed.

crossReferences.why: The second use of the same emphatic prohibition, about God never breaking His promise.
Warns against reading a delay in reckoning as a favour granted to those who do wrong.
Continues this scene, with the wrongdoers asking for a short deferral of their own.

studies.applyIt: Think of a wrong done to you or near you that nothing was ever done about. You do not have to forgive it today, and you do not have to act. Say the smaller sentence instead: this was seen. Then notice whether the weight of it shifts even slightly.
studies.explainEasier: Do not think God has not noticed what bad people do. He is only giving them time. On that day they will run with their heads up and their eyes wide open. Their hearts will be empty.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Defer Us A Little Longer
studies.meaning: The request is modest, which is what makes it devastating. Not rescue, not reversal, only a short extension, with the promise of what they would do with it. The answer does not refuse. It recalls something they had said. Did you not swear before that there would be no passing away for you. Early scholars note that the reply is a question rather than a verdict. It addresses an oath the speakers had made when they thought their situation was permanent.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Oaths were the strongest thing a person could say. Swearing that one's position would never end was a recognisable form of confidence in a society where standing was everything. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars note that the instruction opening it is to warn people. So the whole scene is presented as something described in advance rather than reported after.

keyTerms.note: The verb means to give notice of something ahead, in time to act. It defines the passage's purpose. What follows is described so that it does not have to be met without preparation.
They ask for a small extension rather than a long one, which concedes that a little would have been enough. The adjective makes the request reasonable, and that is what gives the reply its force.

From a root for shifting and ceasing, used of the sun moving off its highest point. What they had sworn was that their position would never move. That is the ordinary confidence of anyone comfortably placed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A debtor in that society could ask for a delay and often got one. Credit ran on relationships, and everyone expected to need the same courtesy eventually. Deferral was the normal mercy of commercial life. The request in this ayah uses exactly that language. That is why the audience would have felt the reply as the closing of a door they had always assumed was open.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for passing away comes from the root that describes the sun moving off its highest point. That is the moment after noon when the light begins to decline. What they had sworn, in that image, was that their sun would never move. That is why the reply consists only of reminding them that they said it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the failure in an assumption rather than in a doctrine. Nobody in it states a belief about God. They had simply sworn that their situation would not change, and lived accordingly. That is a habit rather than a creed, and it is available to anyone. The instruction to warn also makes the scene practical. It is given in advance so that the assumption can be examined while there is still time.

crossReferences.why: The same request for a short delay, made at death, and the same answer that no soul is deferred.
The deferral this ayah's speakers are experiencing, named a few ayat earlier as postponement.
Another version of the plea to be sent back, refused with a word about what lies behind them.

studies.applyIt: Name the thing you would do if you knew you had one more year. Then do the smallest version of it this week. Not the whole thing. The scene in this ayah turns on people who had a great deal of time and an assumption that there would be more. That is the ordinary condition rather than an unusual one.
studies.explainEasier: The people ask God for just a little more time. They say they will listen and do better. God reminds them of something. They once swore that their good life would never end.

studies.title: You Lived In Their Houses
studies.meaning: Three things are put to them, and none of them is a doctrine. You lived where those people lived. It became clear to you what happened to them. And we set out the comparisons for you. Every item is an experience rather than an argument. The charge is that all three were available and none produced a change. Early scholars note the phrase about wronging themselves. That is how the Quran usually describes such peoples, since the damage they did fell first on their own community.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The routes north and south passed the remains of settlements the Arabs knew by name. They associated them with peoples who had rejected their prophets. Traders camped in such places. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars treat the dwellings as those of the earlier peoples named in this surah. Their ruins were part of the Meccan mental furniture rather than distant history.

keyTerms.note: The verb for living in a place, from the root that also gives stillness and calm. Using it of the houses of a destroyed people is pointed. The audience had rested exactly where others had ended.

The Quran's standard formula for such peoples. Wrongdoing is described as landing first on the doer. So the ruins are presented as self-inflicted rather than as an outside judgement falling on the innocent.

The verb means to strike, used as an idiom for presenting an example. Comparisons are named as a third kind of evidence, beside living somewhere and seeing what happened. That puts parables on the same footing as sight.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ruined settlements were ordinary features of the trade roads: walls standing, wells that still gave water, tombs cut into rock. Caravans stopped at them because the water was there. A man could spend a night inside the house of a vanished people and be on his way at dawn without giving it a thought. That is precisely the habit this ayah names.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah names three separate kinds of evidence in a single sentence. They are having lived in the places concerned, having had the outcome made clear, and having been given comparisons. The Quran often stacks its arguments this way. Here the effect is to leave the listener no kind of proof they can claim was missing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats knowledge as something that can be fully held and entirely unused. Nothing was withheld from these hearers. They had the site, the story and the parable. That is a specific account of how people fail, and it is not about information. What the ayah implies is that evidence changes nobody by itself. That is why the surah keeps returning to attention rather than to proof.

crossReferences.why: Names the earlier peoples whose dwellings this ayah says its audience had been living in.
Sends the listener to travel and look at the outcome for those who came before them.
Describes two peoples whose dwellings were made clear to a later generation that walked among them.

studies.applyIt: Think of a warning you have already received in three forms. Someone told you, you watched it happen to a friend, and you have read it somewhere. Pick the one that keeps recurring. This ayah's whole charge is that having the evidence and doing nothing is the normal case, not the unusual one.
studies.explainEasier: You lived in the same houses as people who were destroyed long ago. You saw what happened to them. God even gave you examples to think about. Still nothing changed.

studies.title: Even If Mountains Moved
studies.meaning: Their planning is granted its full size and then placed somewhere. They planned their plan, and their plan is with God, even were it a plan to move mountains. Early scholars note the concessive clause. The ayah does not say the schemes were feeble. Then the second half turns to the reader with the same emphatic prohibition used a few ayat earlier. Never suppose that God will break His promise to His messengers. The reassurance is stated as a warning against a thought rather than as a comfort.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a period when the plans against the community were real, coordinated and effective in the short term. No reversal was visible. No occasion is reported for these ayat. Early scholars note that the promise being defended is the one made to messengers rather than a general assurance. This surah has already shown such a promise made to earlier prophets under a threat of expulsion.

keyTerms.note: A verb followed by its own cognate noun, which in Arabic gives the act its full weight. The construction concedes that the planning was thorough, before the ayah says anything about its outcome.

keyTerms.gloss: and their scheme is with God
keyTerms.note: The preposition means in the presence of, or in the keeping of. Their plan is described as held rather than defeated. That is quieter than saying it will fail, and harder to argue with.

A construction meaning possessor of redress. The Quran uses it sparingly, and always where a promise to the wronged is being defended. So the name is about putting things right rather than about anger.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mountains were the standing image of what does not move. Directions were given by them, borders ran along them, and a family knew the same peaks its great-grandfather had known. To speak of a plan able to shift mountains was to name the largest scale of human intent. That was as large as an Arabian listener could picture. And then to say it was still held in a hand.
studies.didYouKnow: The emphatic prohibition opening the second of these ayat is the same construction used five ayat earlier. There the reader was told never to suppose God unaware of what wrongdoers do. The pair bracket the passage between them. So a section about postponement and pleading is enclosed by two warnings against the same kind of conclusion.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Hope is defended here by an argument about custody rather than about strength. The schemes are not called weak, and the outcome is not described. What is said is where the plan is held. That leaves the timing entirely open, which is honest about the experience of waiting. The second ayah then makes confidence a duty of thought. It aims at the exact conclusion a discouraged person is most likely to reach.

crossReferences.why: The first of the paired prohibitions, warning against supposing God unaware of wrongdoing.
The promise to messengers this ayah defends, given under a threat of expulsion.
Sets human scheming beside God's planning, and names Him the best of planners.

studies.applyIt: Take the thing arranged against you that you keep turning over: the decision made about you, the group that closed ranks. Say one sentence about it today that does not predict an outcome. Not it will work out, but this is held. The difference is small, and it is the difference between hope and a forecast.
studies.explainEasier: These people made big plans against God's messengers. Even a plan big enough to move mountains is held in God's hand. God will never break the promise he made to his messengers.

studies.title: The Earth Changed For Another
studies.meaning: One sentence removes the setting. The earth is exchanged for another earth, and the heavens with it. Then everyone comes out into the open before God. Early scholars differ on what the new earth is. Some describe a changed version of this one, others something wholly other. The classical sources record the range without settling it. What is not in dispute is the effect of the ayah's order. The scenery goes first, and only then are the people described, standing with nothing familiar left around them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Descriptions of the Hour in the Meccan surahs are short, physical and placed at the end of an argument. That is exactly where this one sits. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars note that it closes the section begun several ayat earlier with the promise that God is not unaware. They note that the two divine names at its end were used once before in this surah.

keyTerms.note: A passive from the verb for swapping one thing for another. The same root came earlier in this surah, of people who swapped God's blessing for ingratitude. Here the swap is done to the world.
The verb for emerging onto clear ground. It occurs twice in the Quran, and both are in this surah. So the same image opens and closes its account of that day.

The pair of names Joseph reached for in an Egyptian prison, asking whether scattered lords were better than one. Here they are the names before which everyone stands, with the question no longer open.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The land was the one fixed thing. Tribes were named for their territory, routes were remembered by landmarks, and a man's sense of where he stood in the world was literal. Everything else could be lost in a season. An ayah that replaces the ground itself removes the last item on a certain list. It was the list of things an Arabian listener assumed could not be taken away.
studies.didYouKnow: The two divine names that close this ayah are the same pair a prisoner used in the previous surah. He asked his fellow inmates whether many scattered lords were better than one God who is utterly dominant. The question is asked in a cell in one surah. The next surah answers it with a scene of judgement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage strips away the setting before it says anything about the people. That is a specific claim about what that day removes. Every human position is held in relation to something: a place, a role, a family, a piece of ground. None of that is present. What remains is a name for God that means unopposed. The surah has been arguing towards this since its first ayah about being brought out.

crossReferences.why: The first use of the same verb for emerging before God, opening this surah's account of that day.
Joseph uses the same pair of divine names in prison, as a question rather than a scene.
Describes the same replacement of earth and heavens at greater length, with the same names.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing about your surroundings that quietly tells you who you are: a desk, a city, a room in your parents' house. Picture the sentence in this ayah applied to it. Not to unsettle yourself, but to check what is underneath. Whatever answer comes up is worth thirty seconds of attention today.
studies.explainEasier: One day the earth will be swapped for a different earth, and the sky too. Then everyone will stand out in the open in front of God. He is the One, and nothing can stand against him.

studies.title: Bound Together In Chains
studies.meaning: Three short ayat, and the third explains the first two. The images come first: figures linked together in fetters, garments of pitch, faces covered by fire. Then comes the reason, stated as an accounting rule. So that God may repay each soul what it earned. Early scholars note the tension the passage sets up on purpose. The punishment is described as shared and chained together, while the purpose names each soul separately. The last clause adds that the reckoning itself is swift.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Chains and captivity were familiar from raiding and from the slave trade. Pitch was a substance every traveller knew from waterproofing skins and vessels. No occasion is reported for these ayat. Early scholars note that the passage closes a long section on those who set up rivals to God. The imagery is drawn entirely from things the audience handled rather than from anything exotic.

keyTerms.note: A participle for things fastened in pairs, used of animals yoked side by side. The people who followed each other and argued about it earlier in this surah are described here as physically attached.
A dark, sticky substance used to coat vessels and to treat mange in camels. It occurs only here in the Quran. It burns readily, which is why the next clause follows as it does.
A name that turns a fear into a mercy of sorts. An account settled quickly is not drawn out. The Quran uses this name where the scale of what must be reckoned might otherwise seem impossible.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Pitch was a working substance, not an image. It was smeared on waterskins and boats, and rubbed onto a camel's skin to treat disease. Everyone knew its smell, its blackness and how fast it took a flame. Captives roped together were an ordinary sight after a raid. Both details come from the household and the road rather than from anywhere strange.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for pitch occurs only once in the Quran, in this passage. It names a substance used to treat a camel's skin disease and to seal vessels. So the garment described is made of a familiar thing. An Arabian listener linked it with coating something completely and with catching fire at once.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The final ayah reframes everything before it. What has been described in the language of imprisonment is named as repayment for what each soul earned. That makes it an accounting rather than a display of force. That is the Quran's consistent framing, and it matters because it grounds the whole scene in what people actually did. The name closing the passage, swift in reckoning, keeps the process from being drawn out.

crossReferences.why: The followers and leaders whose argument this scene answers, now described as fastened together.
The instruction that arrives at the same point: do not blame me, blame yourselves.
States the same accounting principle, that each soul is repaid what it earned, with the same name.

studies.applyIt: Look at one thing you do because of who you do it with, and ask whether you would still do it alone. Not a large thing. This passage links people who were joined in a habit, and then names an accounting that is entirely individual. That is worth holding in mind at the next gathering.
studies.explainEasier: On that day people who did wrong are chained together. Their clothes are made of tar and fire covers their faces. God pays each person back for what they did. He settles the account fast.

studies.title: A Notice For All People
studies.meaning: The surah closes by naming what it has been. It is a notice delivered to people, with three purposes joined in a row. That they may be warned, that they may know He is one God, and that those with understanding may take it to heart. Early scholars note the widening. The first purpose reaches everyone. The second is a matter of knowledge. The third narrows to one kind of listener. What began as a book sent to bring people out of darkness ends as a message delivered.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a surah that had opened by stating the purpose of revelation. It then moved through Moses, the earlier peoples, two parables and a sequence of Abraham's prayers. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars note that the word for people here is the general one rather than a term for any one community. That matches the surah's argument that every messenger was sent to his own people.

keyTerms.note: From the root for reaching a destination. It names a message that has arrived rather than a body of teaching. So the emphasis falls on the delivery being complete. The phrase occurs only here.

keyTerms.gloss: and so that they may know
keyTerms.note: Knowledge is named as a purpose alongside being warned. The Quran treats the oneness of God as something to be known rather than only believed. That is why arguments and signs appear throughout this surah.
The second word means the innermost part of a seed, what remains when the shell comes off. It names people who reach the core of a matter. It also closes the surah before this one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A message in that world was delivered, not published. A man carried it and repeated it in the words he had been given. His responsibility ended when it reached the person addressed. Whether it was acted on was not his affair. The word closing this surah is the ordinary term for that transaction. It places the whole book in a familiar and modest category.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah ends on the same phrase for people of understanding that closes the surah before it. So two surahs in a row finish by naming the same audience. The surah of Joseph ends by calling its story a lesson for them. This one ends by asking them to take its notice to heart.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is described at the close as a delivery rather than an achievement. That sets a limit on what a messenger is responsible for. Three outcomes are named, and they get narrower in turn. Warning reaches everyone. Knowledge is available to anyone who examines the case. Taking it to heart belongs to those who get to the core of things. Nothing in the sequence is described as automatic.

crossReferences.why: The surah's opening statement of purpose, which this closing ayah answers and completes.
The previous surah closes by naming the same people of understanding, at the end of its story.
Uses the same word to define a messenger's task as delivery, with God knowing what is concealed.

studies.applyIt: Deliver one message this week and stop there. Say the true thing to the person who needs it, once, in their words, and then leave the outcome alone. Most of the strain in trying to help someone comes from staying past the delivery. This ayah names the point where a messenger's work ends.
studies.explainEasier: This book is a message given to all people. It is there to warn them. It is there so they learn that God is one. People who think deeply will take it to heart.
